analysis.one_liner: Strips federal funding from EPA and Interior reviews of Appalachian coal mining permits until the rules are redone through formal public comment.
analysis.headline: The bill attracted no cosponsors, was referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee, and died there without a vote when the 111th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: In 2009-2010, the EPA and the Army Corps adopted procedures to more closely review surface coal mining permits in Appalachia, including mountaintop-removal mining, under the Clean Water Act. This bill would have cut off federal money for carrying out those procedures until the agencies went through the full, lengthy public-comment rulemaking process to formalize them. In practice, it would have paused the tougher permit reviews. It was introduced by one senator with no cosponsors, sent to the Environment and Public Works Committee, and never heard from again.
analysis.who_benefits: Coal mining companies, especially Appalachian surface-mining operators, would gain the most: the bill would clear away the EPA review procedures that had held up permits for 190 mining operations. The 17,806 mining jobs and 81 small businesses the bill cites would benefit if those permits moved forward. Coal-fired utilities would benefit from a larger domestic coal supply. Electricity customers would benefit only if slower coal permitting were actually driving up power prices, which the bill asserts but does not prove.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Appalachian coal mining companies and suppliers

how_it_helps.text: The bill would bar the EPA, the Army Corps of Engineers, and the Interior Department's mining office from using any funds to carry out the June 2009 permit-coordination memorandum or the April 2010 Appalachian mining review guidance until each was redone through formal notice-and-comment rulemaking.

The bill's findings argue the procedures had delayed Clean Water Act permits for 190 coal mining operations expected to yield over 2 billion tons of coal and support roughly 17,806 jobs and 81 small businesses.
The bill frames the outcome as protecting electricity reliability, claiming coal supplies about half the nation's electricity and that blocking a two-year coal supply would drive up energy prices.

analysis.who_pays: Communities in Appalachia living downstream of surface mines would bear the cost while the stricter permit reviews were suspended, since the procedures the bill targets were written to scrutinize mining's impact on streams and water quality under the Clean Water Act [S2][S3]. Taxpayers fund the agencies whose oversight would be curtailed. Anyone affected by greater air and water pollution from newly approved mines would pay indirectly.

drawbacks.text: The bill would have blocked EPA, the Corps, and OSMRE from enforcing their 2009-2010 Appalachian mining review procedures until formal regulations were issued, removing the main federal check on mountaintop-removal mining's damage to streams and water quality in the interim.

The bill's own findings rest entirely on the coal industry's account of the harm, asserting that EPA 'unlawfully delayed' permits for 190 mining operations and threatened roughly one in four Appalachian coal jobs, without an independent analysis of the environmental cost of approving those permits.

A funding cutoff has no end date: the bill would bar agencies from using their guidance indefinitely until each one completed a full notice-and-comment rulemaking, which could take years, leaving permit reviews in limbo in the meantime.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offered real benefits to one group: coal mining companies and Appalachian mining towns facing delayed permits, lost income, and job risk under the new EPA review procedures [S3]. The cost would fall on downstream communities, whose protection from mountaintop-removal mining damage under the Clean Water Act would be weakened while agencies reworked their rules, and on anyone exposed to the air and water pollution the tighter reviews were designed to catch [S2][S3]. The procedural argument for notice-and-comment rulemaking is legitimate, but as written the bill would have suspended existing oversight indefinitely with no deadline for replacement rules. On balance, the drawbacks outweighed the benefits for the broader public.

outcome.mechanism: A single senator introduced the bill, the Environment and Public Works Committee never acted on it, and it expired when the two-year congressional session ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Jim Bunning introduced S. 3933 on September 29, 2010, in the final months of the 111th Congress.
No senator signed on as a cosponsor.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Environment and Public Works the same day; the committee took no further action recorded in the bill's history.
The 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011, and the bill died without a floor vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The EPA's tougher review of Appalachian surface-mining permits stayed in place, so downstream communities and everyone who drinks from the affected watersheds kept that protection; the coal companies seeking those 190 permits did not get the relief they wanted.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: EPA oversight and communities near mining sites

for.name: Jim Bunning
for.role: U.S. Senator from Kentucky (retiring at the end of the 111th Congress)
for.what_they_did: Sole sponsor; introduced the bill on September 29, 2010, near the end of his final Senate term.

against.name: Barbara Boxer
against.role: Chair, Senate Environment and Public Works Committee
against.what_they_did: Her committee received the bill on referral and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or floor action.

sides.party_line_note: Only one senator, a retiring Kentucky Republican, supported the bill; with zero cosponsors from either party, no partisan pattern can be measured.

industries.industry: Coal mining companies (especially Appalachian surface and mountaintop-removal operators)
industries.note: The bill would lift the EPA review procedures that were delaying permits for 190 mining operations, letting projects and their revenue move forward. Its gain would come at the expense of the water-quality oversight those communities live downstream of.

Utilities would benefit from a larger, more secure coal supply and less regulatory pressure on their fuel source. But the bill would not change fuel economics, and its practical effect on electricity prices was speculative.
